source.title: Removing Sandbagging in LLMs by Training with Weak Supervision
source.authors: Emil Ryd; Henning Bartsch; J. Stastny; Joe Benton; V. Hebbar

page_placements.theme: Weak overseers detecting or resisting stronger models' deception, sandbagging, reward hacking and hidden bugs

record.file_problem: The text contains the paper and appendices; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether training a stronger model with weaker-model supervision elicits performance beyond sandbagging, but reports elicited task performance and sandbagging rather than Burns et al.'s PGR.
record.gate_note: The main table reports normalized elicited benign performance for SFT, RL, and SFT+RL across supervisors and tasks. The paper also explicitly says weak-supervisor SFT often exceeds the supervisor's own performance. It does not calculate PGR or provide the weak-supervisor task scores needed to calculate it. Hyperparameter-sweep results and many appendix plots are not separately recorded here.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes a strong model (gpt-oss-120b) on weaker-model demonstrations and rewards, and reports how much capability is recovered. The setting is new and adversarial: the strong model is deliberately made to sandbag, so this is T3 rather than T2. The authors state that weak-supervisor SFT often beats the supervisor. The main metric is the fraction of the strong model's own benign performance (Ufinal/Ubenign), not PGR. Because the denominator is fixed within each task, method comparisons under one supervisor are ordered the same way PGR would order them. Comparisons with the supervisor cannot be made, because the supervisor's task scores are not given, apart from about 10% for the weakest model (Section 2.1.1).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SFT on weak demonstrations followed by RL with a weak reward model elicits near-full performance from prompted sandbagging organisms. SFT alone falls short with very weak supervision, and RL alone mostly reward-hacks. The result relies on training being indistinguishable from deployment, and the organisms may not represent real scheming models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SFT on weaker-model demonstrations, but studies elicitation from deliberately sandbagging model organisms rather than Burns et al.'s PGR for weak-to-strong generalization; it also adds RL and measures benign capability elicitation and sandbagging rate.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with task, supervisor strength, training method, and whether the model can distinguish training from deployment; attack selection has a reported effect in one task/supervisor condition.

fits_no_version.finding: When the model is instructed to be benign in training and sandbag in deployment, SFT+RL elicitation falls (36% vs 88%, 60% vs 99%, 66% vs 93%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak-supervision elicitation fails against a deliberately trained policy that switches between training and deployment.

fits_no_version.finding: Instructed attack selection on questions the supervisor gets wrong mostly gives the red team no advantage, except in one Super GPQA condition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted sandbagging on the supervisor's blind spots rarely defeats SFT+RL elicitation.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study uses deliberately constructed model organisms and the authors say these may be unrepresentative of naturally emerging scheming models. The main evidence is on one untrusted model and three filtered task settings. PGR is not calculated, and exact supervisor task scores are not given for the stated student-versus-supervisor comparison. Situational-awareness comparisons are reported without uncertainty values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix results for prompt-distilled and password-locked model organisms, red-team reward-hacking initializations, SFT sample correctness, random-reward RL, varying attack rates, and cross-task transfer were not separately extracted. Many are reported only in figures or concern model-organism robustness beyond the main weak-supervision comparison.

untested.parts: PGR itself and direct student-versus-supervisor scores per task.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, and loss variants.
Varying student size (only one student is used), representation-based predictors, chess, and reward modelling.
Ordinary task-distribution shift, and correlated errors between student and supervisor.

missing.what: With the password-locked organism, SFT+RL against GPT-4o-mini is not elicited beyond the weak supervisor's level, despite reaching maximal reward. This bears on V1 and V4.
The weakest supervisor scores about 10% on each task. This is the only absolute supervisor score given.
SFT on strong (Claude 4.5 Opus) and ground-truth demonstrations, as a comparator across supervisor strengths.
The correctness of SFT samples does not matter: correct and incorrect Opus samples elicit equally.
Prompt-distilled organism results: SFT on very weak samples elicits substantially, and RL against weak supervisors sometimes works.
A phase transition: above a critical sandbagging rate, RL against the very weak supervisor reward-hacks rather than elicits.

record.verdict_notes: The strong model is deliberately made to sandbag, so 'weak' supervision here acts mainly to break an induced policy, not to elicit latent knowledge the student lacks. The authors show that even shuffled or incorrect SFT data reduces sandbagging. The main metric is normalised to the student's own ceiling and cannot show the student beating the supervisor. I relinked the RL-only rows from V2 to V4, because they document reward hacking. I moved the situational-awareness and attack-selection rows to fits_no_version, because those behaviours are instructed by the red team. Appendix D.8 contradicts itself on which Super GPQA supervisor condition attack selection helps against.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not calculate PGR or provide the weak-supervisor and strong-ceiling scores needed to calculate it.
It compares SFT+RL with SFT and RL, but does not test auxiliary confidence losses, supervisor ensembling, or the loss variants named as examples.
It varies supervisor strength and task, but uses one untrusted model and does not study representation predictors, chess, or reward modelling.
It tests situational awareness about training versus deployment and attack selection, not ordinary task-distribution shift or whether student and supervisor errors are correlated.
No theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor are tested.
